# Jenna Ammerall — Product Designer

> Making products make sense. As a senior product designer with nine years at
> Microsoft and Meta, Jenna gets to the root of the problem, defines the behaviors,
> and builds the frameworks teams need to carry those decisions across
> products—so everything moves as one. Seattle-based. Focus areas: design systems,
> accessibility, interaction design, platform and information architecture.
> Site: https://ammerallj.design/

Contact: ammerallj@gmail.com · https://www.linkedin.com/in/ammerallj/

## Selected work

- [Shaping Accessibility Across Products](https://ammerallj.design/work/accessibility.html): Meta, Risk Areas / Accessibility, December 2023–July 2026. Design Lead across product systems, interaction design, and AI strategy. Accessibility had relied on specialists catching issues late in development; the European Accessibility Act made it business-critical, and reviewing after the fact couldn't keep up with AI-accelerated build cycles. The deeper problem: a standard only becomes real when people can find it, apply it, verify it, and trust it—and at Meta's scale, none of that happened on its own. What changed: product teams could apply the accessibility standard during design and build, with a playbook that translated 29 requirements into 23 practical topics organized around the decisions teams were already making; accessibility review stopped being a manual bottleneck, as shared workflows reduced the manual coordination required across program managers, reviewers, and product teams, while automated checks cut a recurring 3–5 hour review to effectively zero per wave and a separate submission workflow saved 1,711 hours; product teams could go from an accessibility question to the guidance that applied without searching through 200+ pages, reducing deprecated results from 25% to zero; people could find accessibility support in one place for the first time, as a needs-based model became a customer-facing experience bringing 30+ features and 45 Help Center articles into a single path on meta.com. Full case study is confidential; the public destination is live at https://www.meta.com/accessibility/

- [Creating Continuity Across Messaging](https://ammerallj.design/work/messaging.html): Meta, Facebook Messaging, April–December 2023. Design Lead across interaction design and product strategy. On Facebook, private sharing is how conversations start—a Reel or listing sent to one person—but continuing meant replying in Messenger, and entry points designed in isolation made conversations less predictable. What changed: in-app messaging had a shared model across Facebook surfaces (a reusable interaction model covering 11 entry points on iOS and Android, defining how conversations begin, confirm and continue, which continued guiding rollout after handoff); large-scale switching between Facebook and Messenger was reduced, addressing 100M+ monthly app switches; and people were more likely to continue the conversation after sending, at +21.9% thread opens on iOS and +27.1% on Android with neutral topline metrics. Scope note: ownership was localized to Jenna's org and leadership, not Meta's messaging ecosystem. Full case study is confidential.

- [Giving Components an Identity](https://ammerallj.design/work/microsoft-loop.html): Microsoft, Loop, May 2020–March 2022. UX Designer across interaction, platform, and visual design. Microsoft Loop introduced live components that could move across Microsoft 365; the hard part was making one read as the same live thing in every app it landed in. What changed: a Loop component could remain itself wherever it lived, via a persistent interaction model for identity, sharing, and connections that became part of the patented model for shared dynamic objects (US 12,277,305); collaborative components moved from concept into Microsoft 365, the first shipping in Teams as synchronized tables, lists, agendas, and action items (debuting at Ignite 2021); and the component structure became something others could build to, its header and boundary later appearing in Microsoft's public developer guidance.

- [Helping People Navigate Communities](https://ammerallj.design/work/facebook-groups.html): Meta, Facebook Groups, March 2022–April 2023. Product Designer across interaction design, design systems, and design quality. Most people on Facebook belong to at least 15 active groups and more than 100 million join one every day; people needed clearer ways to navigate between communities without losing context. What changed: people could move through Groups with clearer orientation and context (+0.26% engagement on a mature consumer surface); core Groups experiences became more consistent across platforms, with design-system adoption reaching ~82% across iOS and Android; and implementation quality improved across core surfaces, with 17 implementation reviews with engineering and 200+ UI issues resolved.
